paragraphs: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah. (a) Mishnah Avot, end of chapter 3. Further references (chapter:mishnah): Berakhot 1:5;4:7. Shevi'it 1:8;3:3. Ma'aserot 5:1. Ma'aser Sheni 5:9. Shabbat 4:2;5:4;19:3. Eruvin 4:1. Yoma 8:9. Beitzah 2:8. Mo'ed Katan 1:2. Ketubbot 4:6;5:1. Nedarim 3:11. Nazir 6:2. Sotah 9:15. Bava Kamma 6:4. Makkot 1:10. Eduyot 3:12. Zevachim 1:3. Menachot 13:6. Arakhin 8:4. Keritot 2:5. Kelim 3:8. Nega'im 7:2;8:9;13:6. Mikvaot 3:2;8:3. Yadayim 3:5;4:2,3. Makhshirin 6:6. Tohorot 7:7. Uktzin 1:5.

(b) Wise, wealthy, tenth generation from Ezra, and a priest. When Gamliel of Yavneh was removed, they appointed him nasi at eighteen. A miracle gave him eighteen rows of white hair. He expounded: one should study Torah even without pure motive, eventually reaching pure motive. Four hundred benches were added; some say seven hundred, Berakhot 28. Yuchasin’s chronological section cites Jerusalem Talmud, Tamid Nishchat, for age thirteen. It is not there, but in Berakhot, Tefillat Hashachar, end of mishnah 1, and Ta'anit, chapter 4, end of halakhah 1: “He was sixteen; all his head filled with grey. Akiva sat grieving: ‘He is not more learned than I, but of greater ancestry. Happy is one whose fathers merit for him; happy is one with a peg to hang on!’ His peg was tenth-generation descent from Ezra. How many benches? Scholars’ benches, besides those behind the fence. One says three hundred, besides,” etc. “When they agreed to restore Gamliel, Elazar ben Azaryah rose early with them to Gamliel’s door. They did not remove his dignity, but appointed him court head.” End quotation. Yefeh Mar'eh, Tefillat Hashachar, gloss 8: Babylonian Merubbeh says Yehoshua was Gamliel’s court head, so Elazar ben Azaryah was not court head; after restoration Gamliel expounded two Shabbats, Azaryah one. (Sh.K., 22b [בש״ק; work unresolved], says Yehoshua was with Gamliel forty years.) Yuchasin: “We shall not abandon the plain sense: he exceeded seventy, saying ‘I am like seventy.’ The Jerusalem Talmud does not discuss ‘like seventy.’” End quotation. I do not understand: if literally seventy, why ‘like’? Perhaps appointed at eighteen or sixteen, but seventy when expounding the nighttime Exodus mention, without gaining agreement until ben Zoma expounded it. Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, chapter 1: “I am like seventy”; though attaining high office, he lived long. End quotation. Yefeh Mar'eh, section 19: this contradicts the Babylonian account, where eighteen white rows appeared on the day “they appointed R.Y.” [לר״י; identity/wording unresolved], prompting “like seventy.”

(c) Shabbat 54b: he tithed twelve thousand calves annually. Tosafot object: Bekhorot 53a says animal tithing ceased after destruction. He therefore tithed during the Temple’s time, presumably at least thirteen, since minors cannot tithe. At destruction he could only be fourteen or fifteen: Zakkai remained nasi one or two years afterward (see there); Gamliel then one, two, or three before Azaryah’s appointment, since Tefillat Hashachar says “last year,” at Rosh Hashanah, he distressed him. Appointed at eighteen, he was at most fourteen or fifteen before destruction; for only two tithing years, why “every year”? Answer: his guardian tithed for him. Alternatively, abolition came some years after destruction. Rabbi Elchanan: afterward he paid royal arnona, a levy. See Tosafot there and Bekhorot; Avodah Zarah 13a; Yoma 66a; Beitzah 23a. There the Gemara reads thirteen thousand, while Tosafot in those places have twelve thousand.

(d) Yevamot 86b: Akiva says terumah to a priest, first tithe to a Levite; Azaryah says to a priest too. Akiva turned the entrance of a garden providing Azaryah first tithe toward a cemetery. “Akiva with his bag, while I live!” he said. Jerusalem Talmud, Ma'aser Sheni, chapter 5, halakhah 3: Yehoshua says tithe is not given to a priest; Azaryah says it is; Yehoshua told him, etc.; Azaryah told him, etc. A garden from which Azaryah took tithe had two entrances, one toward impurity, one purity. Akiva told the owner to close the pure entrance and open the impure one, directing Azaryah through it. “Perhaps he will send a nonpriest agent.” “Say the verse says ‘you’—he must take it himself, not through an agent.” Azaryah heard: “Akiva’s stratagems have come here!” He returned all the tithes he had taken; see there. They listed him before Akiva despite Akiva’s being greater because of his lineage (see Akiva). He told Akiva, “Though you multiply derivations all day, I will not listen,” Menachot 89a [printed: 29a]; Niddah 72b.

(e) Bekhorot 58a: ben Azzai says all Israel’s sages are like garlic peels to him, except this bald man. Tosafot, citing Jerusalem Talmud: Azaryah, who was bald; see Yehoshua ben Korcha and Akiva. End of Sotah: with his death wealth ceased among sages. Berakhot 57b: seeing him in a dream portends wealth. Shabbat 54b: his neighbor’s cow once went out on Shabbat with a strap between its horns; he failed to protest, and fasting blackened his teeth. Sefer Hammikhtam says a festival. Jerusalem Talmud: his wife was called his cow, as “Had you not plowed with my heifer.” She went out wearing something the sages forbade, disparagingly called his cow; cow and calf are one matter. He expounded in Yavneh’s vineyard, Ketubbot 49; Bava Batra 131b; Kohelet Rabbah 2:8 [printed: 6]. Yevamot 16a: Dosa ben Hyrcanus asked, “Has our colleague Azaryah a son?”, see there, and applied “I was young and have grown old.” Jerusalem Talmud, Yevamot, chapter 1, halakhah 6, has Yonatan ben Hyrcanus apply it: “I know him, tenth generation from Ezra.” Called a basket of spices, Gittin 67a. On his appointment day were Yishmael, Yehoshua ben Matya, and Yose Dormaskit. He called Yishmael “my brother,” Berakhot 11a; Tarfon too, Yadayim, chapter 4. R.Ch. [ר״ח; authority unresolved] says Eliezer was his teacher. Shemot Rabbah, Mishpatim: he went to Rome with Gamliel, Yehoshua, and Akiva; his father Azaryah was wise and wealthy, see there. Tosafot, Yevamot 86a: he was much earlier than Meir. Tosefta, Kelim, Bava Batra, chapter 2: Yehoshua recounts four elders before Azaryah—Chutzpit, Yeshevav, Chalafta, Yochanan ben Nuri. Gilgulei Neshamot, Alef 4: Azaryah reincarnated Ezra, and Ibn Ezra reincarnated Azaryah. Gilgulei Neshamot, Pe 11, identifies the cow as a rectification of Korach’s wife (fitting Jerusalem Talmud’s cow-as-wife), who advised him about an all-blue cloak; the horn-strap hints at its four corners, also called horns. His grave is at Kefar Alma (see Elazar ben Arakh); Benjamin’s Travels places it at Kedesh Naphtali in the Asher edition [the Adler edition places it at Alma], see that entry.

(f) In Elazar Hammodai’s name. Boethus ben Zunin in his time; Dosa ben Hyrcanus (see there). Yehudah son of Ilai, his student. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha reports in his name [printed: ריב״ק]. Yose the Galilean; Yose ben Kippur in his name. His son Yishmael. Levi Hassarad in his time. Rav Shezvi in his name; Resh Lakish in his name. Shimon, Azaryah’s brother, his uncle. Rav Sheshet in his name.
